job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Nikhil Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Nikhil. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Wake up at eight, check what my Discord bot broke overnight, then lectures for my master's in AI and robotics at Tidewater University. Between classes I ask an AI assistant to explain whatever I didn't follow, and I use another one to draft my code. Afternoons I work the repair counter at a phone kiosk in the Harbour Mall, 20 hours a week, and evenings I tinker with a small robot arm in the shared kitchen of my student house. My flatmates complain about the soldering smell.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Computer science, a pass. I ran a little Discord bot for a gaming community that brought in about 150 a month, and honestly I spent more time on that than on lectures. My final project was a path planner for a warehouse robot, and it worked in simulation but I wrote it up badly. No internship. My parents run the kitchen at a restaurant and work six days a week, so no money from them, and I owe about thirty thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful and overrated at the same time. I use it every day and it saves me an hour or two, but it still writes confident nonsense about a third of the time. I'd tell my flatmates: learn it, don't worship it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it changes little for me, and that's a problem, because my money situation is bad whether AI is real or not. Thirty thousand in debt, no internship, and robotics jobs near here are mostly at two firms. I'm good with the tools, but a pass degree still gets filtered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep the kiosk job and grow the bot's subscriber list from 120 to 300. I'd put the robot arm project on video and send it to both local robotics firms. I'd apply to ten places a week and track every result in a sheet, because I like data about what works. I'd also try a hackathon or two, since they're a way to get noticed without grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless. I'm fine in myself, but money anxiety nags, like a notification I can't clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it writes nonsense a third of the time. How does that change how you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check everything. If I let it write code, I run the tests first and read the diff after. People who don't do that end up with bugs they can't explain, and I've seen it in my own class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you grow the bot from 120 to 300 subscribers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Offer a free trial and ask the community moderators for a shout-out. I'd also add one feature people ask for, a tournament scheduler. At 3 a month each, 300 subscribers is 900 a year more, which would cover my train pass.

I'd tell flatmates it writes confident nonsense about a third of the time.
think: My **money** situation is bad whether AI is real or not: thirty thousand in debt and few robotics jobs near here.
Being good with the tools doesn't fix a **pass degree**.

Film the **robot arm** project and send it to both local robotics firms.
Apply to ten places a week and track every result in a **sheet**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the real deal, and that most people are underestimating the pace. The writing, coding and checking tasks go to software first, and a lot of junior roles are those tasks. I'd say, though, that it's also a chance if you build things instead of waiting for a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a decent position and a worse one than my classmates realise. I'm good with the tools, so I could be the junior a small team keeps. But the pass grade and no internship still make me easy to filter out, and entry jobs shrink. My honest guess is a one-in-two chance of a proper first job within a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean into robotics, because hands-on work is slower to be automated and my robot arm skills are real. I'd try to get a role at a robotics integrator or a warehouse automation firm. I'd keep the bot going for income. I'd also contribute to an open-source robotics project, where good work is visible. And I'd stay at the kiosk until something paid more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little jittery, mostly in a good way. Change suits me, but the debt makes it harder to enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one in two. What would improve the odds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Having a demo that works in a real place. If I can get my path planner running on a real cart in a real warehouse, even for a day, that's worth ten applications. I'd offer to do a free trial for a small warehouse near the port.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it went the other way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take a technician job at one of the integrators, even if it's far from design work. A paid foot in the door beats a clever idea in a cupboard. And I'd keep tinkering at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is mind-blowing and honestly scary. I'd say we're not ready, that there should be an emergency policy discussion, and that people should stop pretending the old career ladder is coming back. I'd also say, only half joking, that I'd be building something the day it's announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious, not panicked. Everything that is thinking work, including AI engineering, gets done by AI better and cheaper, and that includes what I'm studying. Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, so physical robotics work might last a bit longer, but the design side goes quick. My debt does not care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work the angle where humans are needed in the loop: installing, maintaining and fixing the robots, wiring them into real places. I'd take any hands-on job in automation, even at low pay. I'd drop the master's if a job came up. I'd also push the bot and any small projects I could sell. And I'd talk to my parents' restaurant about whether any of their kitchen work could use a small robot, since I'd practise on something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired, buzzing. I'd be scared and curious at once, like standing on the top step of a diving board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd practise on your parents' kitchen. What would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the dishwashing line. Dad has a guy who works eight hours there for not much, and an arm that loads racks isn't science fiction. I'd want to try it and see how it fails. And I'd be doing something for my parents for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd be good at something that stops existing. Some people would say that's the case with every new technology, but with AGI the speed is the problem, not the change.

Keep selling subscriptions to the Discord bot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a decent runway. I'd say we should use it to push training, build safety nets and start the policy conversation now. I'd say it in my usual way, a bit nerdy, with a chart, to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but optimistic. If I land a first job in robotics within a year, I'd get roughly three or four years of real experience before AGI hits, and the hands-on side lasts until about 2034. That's enough to build skills, savings and a name. The scary scenario is that I don't land the first job and the door closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and aim for robotics integration work. I'd save 200 a month and clear the high-interest loan first. I'd spend weekends on the robot arm and publish what I learn, which builds a reputation. I'd also keep an eye on what skills the integrators ask for and train in those. And I'd start something small on my own, like selling maintenance contracts for small warehouse robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good-ish. It's like a long exam: scary, but I know what to revise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you chart for people, if you had to explain this scenario?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two lines. One shows thinking jobs falling from 2031, the other shows hands-on jobs falling from 2034. Between them is a gap of three years where the people who can work with the robots are paid well. I'd tell people to find that gap and stand in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the gap isn't there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd fall back on the plan I have for the fast scenarios: any job that touches a machine, a cheap flat, and the bot. I'm never going to have all the answers, but I always have a next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot. I'd say it's time to rethink education and welfare, but I wouldn't lose sleep. I'd say it with a shrug, because over ten years most things change in ways nobody predicts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be mostly relaxed. By 2036 I'd be 34 and could be running my own small robotics outfit or a senior role in one. The debt would be gone. The uncertainty is whether anyone will need a human at all in 2039, but that's far away, and I can't plan for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a robotics integration job, and pay off the loan within about four years. I'd keep building the bot and the arm for fun and for income. I'd move into a role with some hands-on and some management, since both would last longer. I'd also buy a small place with my parents' help, maybe so they can retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. I think I'd look back on it as a decent decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned helping your parents retire. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small flat near the restaurant so they walk to work instead of two buses, and in a few years a smaller shift pattern. They've worked six days a week for twenty years. It's the one thing I'd really want to do with a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be mostly relaxed. What would pull you back to worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I hadn't landed a first job after a year, I'd be worried again straight away. Ten years is a comfort only if the first job goes well. After that, I back myself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. It leaves no time to pay down debt or build a track record, and I'd be competing with software that never sleeps. What would help is public retraining money, apprenticeships in robotics and some protection for people carrying student loans. And more employers willing to look at what you've built instead of the grade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I think people assume graduates who like AI are fine. We're not, we're just faster at noticing the problem. I'd like someone to say that a pass grade with a real project should count.
